title: Wipe away tears (Isaiah 25:6–8)
hook: a feast of rich food for all peoples, and death swallowed up

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malachi, and Elijah sent to turn the hearts of parents and children. Your line: open the door for Elijah.

After a funeral, there's usually food. A long table in a church hall, casseroles under foil, someone's famous potato salad, coffee in big urns. People who haven't seen each other in years stand holding paper plates, and between the tears there's sometimes laughter. Grief and a meal, side by side. Today Isaiah takes that same table and turns it inside out: a feast where the guest list is everyone on earth, and what gets swallowed up at the end of the meal is death.
screen: `GRIEF AND A MEAL, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the menu, in the King James Bible: "a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined." Fat things meant the best food, the richest cuts. Wine on the lees is wine left to age on its sediment until it's deep and smooth. It's a banquet, set on God's mountain, for all people, every nation. Then the feast turns. God removes the covering cast over all peoples, the veil spread over all nations. Some readers hear a burial shroud, the cloth laid over the dead, lifted off the whole human race. And then: "He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces." Some readers hear an echo of older stories from that region, where death was a swallower with a huge mouth. Here, the swallower gets swallowed. After the victory, God doesn't make a speech. God goes face to face, wiping tears off cheeks one by one, like a parent after a nightmare. The New Testament picks these words up twice. Paul quotes the swallowing of death when he writes about the resurrection. And near the very end of the Bible, Revelation says: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes." Christians hear in this feast a picture of what they hope for. This week's prophets walked us here: Habakkuk's yet, the God who sings, a bag with holes, Zerubbabel, the donkey king, hearts turned. And now, a table set for everyone.
screen: then, large: `HE WILL SWALLOW UP DEATH IN VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've lost, or someone grieving now, and let yourself feel it for a moment; Isaiah's feast doesn't skip the tears. Then picture a table and who you'd want at it, someone lonely, someone far from home, and picture setting the plate in front of them. If you pray, give thanks for the people at your table; if not, simply hold them in mind.
Shroud, the burial cloth laid over the dead: Isaiah's picture of God lifting it off every nation at a feast where death is swallowed up.
Your line: tears wiped away. Face by face, one by one. Day four hundred ninety-seven, and another week walked.

howItsDone: Isaiah 25:6–9 is among the funeral readings in some churches, and some Christians connect its feast with the communion meal and with the hope of resurrection.

chat.meaning: Isaiah's banquet is for all people. The shroud over every nation is lifted, death is swallowed up, and God wipes tears from all faces.

lees.meaning: the sediment wine is left to age on

Paul.meaning: the apostle who quotes the swallowing of death

Revelation.meaning: the Bible's last book, which echoes the wiping of tears

notes: Revelation 21:4 KJV reads 'And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes;' — quoted to the semicolon. Revelation 7:17 has a similar line.
The covering/veil of 25:7 as a burial shroud is a common interpretation, presented as 'many readers hear'.
Death as a swallowing figure: Canaanite/Ugaritic Mot is described with an enormous swallowing mouth. Stated generally as 'the old stories of that region'. Confirm.
'Wine on the lees' as wine aged on its sediment. Confirm.
